scenes.title: Where and when
narration: Maloya originated among enslaved populations from Madagascar and East Africa.
It was historically practiced in secret to avoid colonial prohibition.
The genre gained political prominence in the late 1950s, notably through the work of Firmin Viry, and became a symbol of the struggle for autonomy.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Maloya is used for ancestral worship (servis kabaré), political protest, and the celebration of the abolition of slavery on December 20th.
It serves as a moral touchstone and a vehicle for asserting political rights.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: Traditional maloya is defined by a percussion-heavy ensemble.

Key instruments include the roulèr (a low-tuned barrel drum played with hands), the kayamb (a flat rattle made of sugar cane and seeds), the pikér (bamboo idiophone), the sati (metal idiophone), and the bob (a braced, struck musical bow).
Listen for the roulèr, kayamb, pikér, sati.
The pulse is Ternary.
A percussive, rhythmic sound driven by the deep resonance of the roulèr drum and the rattling of the kayamb, accompanied by a vocal soloist leading a choir.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Firmin Viry, Danyèl Waro, Gramoun Lélé, Christine Salem, Ziskakan, Baster, Granmoun Baba, Rwa Kaff, Ti Fock.
Maloya pilé (festive, daily life themes) and maloya roulé (ritualistic, Malagasy influence).
Descends from African and Malagasy musical traditions brought to Réunion by enslaved people; shares origins with séga.
